Subject: Dedicated GPU commitment details — queueing & uptime clarification

Hi Ben,

Thanks for the call earlier. Purchasing sent over the draft and they flagged two areas we need clarified before we move to signatures:

1) Queueing behavior during bursts — your current draft references 'best-effort queuing' for short bursts. We need to understand whether requests will be throttled, queued with FIFO guarantees, or routed to an overflow model variant. CloudScale's SLA requires predictable tail latency for our realtime pricing service.

2) Uptime credits and the measurement window — procurement wants to know how you calculate availability for Dedicated pools (per-pool vs per-region) and whether scheduled maintenance windows are excluded from the SLA.

I've attached a redline of the SLA with comments (CloudScale_SLA_redline_v2.pdf) and a simple diagram of our traffic pattern. Can you loop in your engineering or infra team to confirm the operational behavior and any temporary exceptions you can offer while we ramp?

We are targeting a signed order by end of month; these clarifications are blockers for our legal folks.

Best,
Sarah
Sarah Lopez
Head of Procurement, CloudScale

From: ben_carter@redwood.ai
To: Sarah Lopez <s.lopez@cloudscale.io>
Cc: maya_srinivasan@redwood.ai, vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2026 08:37:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Dedicated GPU commitment details — queueing & uptime clarification

Hi Sarah — thanks for the detailed notes and the redline. Appreciate the diagram; that helps.

Quick answers while I pull in our infra team:
- Queueing behavior: Dedicated pools are capacity-reserved by customer and we prioritize requests from the pool owner. In sustained overload (traffic above committed throughput), requests are queued for up to 2s by default; after that they are routed to a compatible lower-cost burst tier if configured, or rejected with a clear 429. For realtime pricing we can shorten queue window to 250–500ms and enable an overflow routing to a pinned smaller-latency model variant.
- Measurement window & availability: Availability is calculated per-dedicated-pool over a 30-day rolling window. Scheduled maintenance is excluded when announced in the maintenance calendar; emergency maintenance is considered in the window but eligible for different credit treatment.

That said, legal and procurement often ask for an explicit temporary exception for ramp periods — we can offer a 3-month ramp SLA addendum that guarantees an effective throughput headroom (X% above baseline) and a faster internal escalation path. Maya (cc'd) can follow up with a proposed addendum language and the queueing diagram from infra. Vivek, can you confirm whether we can offer the 3-month ramp credit and what the headroom percentage should be at the proposed committed GPU count?

I'll attach the redline back with inline responses and propose times for a follow-up call tomorrow.

Best,
Ben Carter
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: maya_srinivasan@redwood.ai

Hi Sarah, Ben — looping in the SRE/serving product notes below and attaching a simple queueing diagram (queueing_behavior_diagram.png).

On queueing behavior (detailed):
- Dedicated pool requests are admitted to a per-customer request queue on the serving nodes. Admission follows arrival order, but we apply priority to requests that match the committed model+precision profile.
- Queue length is bounded by token-rate backpressure and the per-request latency SLO. We expose two knobs: max_queue_delay (default 2s) and overflow_policy (route|reject).
- For CloudScale's realtime pricing workload we recommend: max_queue_delay = 300ms, overflow_policy = route (to pinned low-latency variant). This keeps p95 tail latency predictable while allowing brief spikes without rejecting traffic.

On throughput credits and measurement:
- SLA availability is measured per-pool: uptime = (total_successful_service_time / total_observed_time) over 30-day window.
- Scheduled maintenance (announced >72 hours ahead) is excluded. Unannounced emergency work is included but we have a different credit tier for emergency outages.

Temporary ramp addendum proposal (3 months):
- Effective headroom: 20% additional allocation for the first 90 days beyond committed vGPU baseline.
- If tail latency exceeds agreed thresholds more than 3 times in a 30-day window during the ramp period, we provide a service credit of 5% of monthly committed fees for that month.

Attaching the redline with inline comments. Ben — if CloudScale is comfortable with the 20% ramp and the 300ms queue window, I can convert this into an addendum draft and route to legal.

Thanks,
Maya Srinivasan
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Ben / Maya,

Thanks for the fast response and for the concrete numbers — that helps a lot. Procurement has reviewed the proposed ramp addendum and asks for two small changes:

1) Ramp headroom to be expressed as "up to 20% additional GPU capacity or equivalent throughput for burst periods", so we can validate against our in-house load-testing metrics.
2) Clarify that the 5% credit is cumulative with standard outage credits (i.e., both can apply), and provide an example calculation in the addendum.

If you can include those clarifications in the addendum PDF, procurement is ready to take the redlined SLA to legal review today. We remain committed to the end-of-month signature if the addendum is included.

I've attached back your redline with legal's marginal notes.
